title: Landslide
wiki_lead:
Landslides, also known as landslips, rockslips, rockfalls, mudslides, mudslips or rockslides, are several forms of mass wasting that may include a wide range of ground movements, such as rockfalls, mudflows, shallow or deep-seated slope failures and debris flows. Landslides occur in a variety of environments, characterized by either steep or gentle slope gradients, from mountain ranges to coastal cliffs or even underwater, in which case they are called submarine landslides.
Gravity is the primary driving force for a landslide to occur, but there are other factors affecting slope stability that produce specific conditions that make a slope prone to failure. In many cases, the landslide is triggered by a specific event (such as heavy rainfall, an earthquake, a slope cut to build a road, and many others), although this is not always identifiable.
Landslides are frequently made worse by human development (such as urban sprawl) and resource exploitation (such as mining and deforestation). Land degradation frequently leads to less stabilization of soil by vegetation. Additionally, global warming caused by climate change and other human impact on the environment, can increase the frequency of natural events (such as extreme weather) which trigger landslides. Landslide mitigation describes the policy and practices for reducing the risk of human impacts of landslides, reducing the risk of natural disaster.
grok_lead: A landslide is the movement of a mass of rock, debris, earth, or other materials down a slope under the influence of gravity, classified as a form of mass wasting. These events encompass various processes, including falls, topples, slides, spreads, and flows, differentiated by the type of material involvedâsuch as rockfalls, debris flows, or earthflowsâand the style of movement, which can be rotational or translational. Landslides vary in scale from localized creep to catastrophic failures displacing millions of cubic meters of material. Landslides are triggered by natural factors like prolonged heavy rainfall saturating slopes, earthquake shaking destabilizing materials, volcanic eruptions melting snow or ejecting debris, and erosion undercutting bases, as well as human activities including slope excavation for roads, deforestation reducing soil cohesion, and improper drainage altering water flow. They predominantly occur in steep terrains with fractured rock, deep or thin soils over bedrock, or areas prone to rapid saturation, and can propagate underwater as submarine landslides. Globally, landslides result in thousands of deaths annually and inflict billions of dollars in property damage, with the United States alone recording 25 to 50 fatalities per year. Significant events, such as those induced by seismic activity or extreme weather, highlight their potential for widespread destruction, underscoring the need for hazard mapping and mitigation strategies like slope stabilization and early warning systems.
